For one product component under the valid null, if λG−1\lambda_{G-1} lies in a common deterministic moment domain of Proposition 8 and the required integrability and 𝔼⁡[𝒱]<∞\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{V}]<\infty hold, the expected log loss is at most log⁡G+12​λG−12​𝔼​[𝒱]\log G+\tfrac{1}{2}\lambda_{G-1}^{2}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{V}]; for a residue-class average, apply Jensen with the class-averaged proxy, under these conditions for every class.

Proposition 11 (Rank calibrators; new).

Let gg be positive and nonincreasing on the Ncand=B+1N_{\mathrm{cand}}=B+1 positions, with mean one; put cg=Ncand−1​∑klog⁡g⁡(k)c_{g}=N_{\mathrm{cand}}^{-1}\sum_{k}\log g(k) and rg=log⁡g⁡(1)−log⁡g⁡(Ncand)r_{g}=\log g(1)-\log g(N_{\mathrm{cand}}). For ei,tR=g⁡(Ri,t)e^{\mathrm{R}}_{i,t}=g(R_{i,t}), with Ri,tR_{i,t} the unique rank of the observed score or a rank drawn by uniform random tie-breaking, let τi,t\tau_{i,t} be the total-variation distance of its conditional law from the uniform one. Then 𝔼⁡[log⁡ei,tR∣ℱt]≤cg+τi,t​rg\mathbb{E}[\log e^{\mathrm{R}}_{i,t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\leq c_{g}+\tau_{i,t}r_{g}, and over TT factors 𝔼⁡[log⁡ER]≤T​cg+rg​∑t𝔼⁡[τi,t]\mathbb{E}[\log E^{\mathrm{R}}]\leq Tc_{g}+r_{g}\sum_{t}\mathbb{E}[\tau_{i,t}]. If gg is not constant, cg<0c_{g}<0 and the bound is negative whenever the average 𝔼⁡[τi,t]\mathbb{E}[\tau_{i,t}] is below −cg/rg-c_{g}/r_{g}.

For the normalized power family of §3.5 with Ncand=128N_{\mathrm{cand}}=128, cg=−0.414c_{g}=-0.414, rg=3.852r_{g}=3.852 and the threshold is 0.10750.1075 for κ=1/ln⁡128\kappa=1/\ln 128 (with log⁡g⁡(1)=2.665\log g(1)=2.665), and −0.142-0.142, 2.4262.426 and 0.05840.0584 for κ=1/2\kappa=1/2. The statistic we use averages gg over tied positions. That keeps the factor’s mean at one, but its null baseline is then a bag-dependent constant between cgc_{g} and zero, equal to zero when all candidates tie (Appendix B.11); the untied price is therefore not the price of the implemented statistic when ties are frequent, as in the Atari games of §9.

4.6 Designs with delayed feedback

Proposition 12 (Delayed feedback; new).
  1. (a)

    Under Assumption 2 and hypotheses (i)–(iii) of Proposition 1, with (iii) drawing from Qi,tQ_{i,t}, the conclusions (a)–(c) of Proposition 1 hold under H0GH_{0}^{G}, and under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}} when the product form holds for the tested set conditionally on the outside blocks.

  2. (b)

    A sufficient condition for Assumption 2, before any eligibility conditioning, is that actions are generated as Ai,s=πi,s​(H⋅,s−L,Ai,<s,Ui,s)A_{i,s}=\pi_{i,s}(H_{\cdot,s-L},A_{i,<s},U_{i,s}) with L≥hL\geq h, where the policies and their parameters are fixed given the permitted information, H⋅,s−LH_{\cdot,s-L} is the history of all units up to time s−Ls-L that the design records (outcomes, logged states and actions), no policy reads another unit’s actions inside the block, and the innovations Ui,sU_{i,s} are mutually independent and independent of ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and of all potential outcomes.

Restricting only the tested units’ policies is not enough under spillovers: an outside unit that reacts to a tested unit’s action inside the block can carry that action into the tested target. A known non-product joint design could support a single jointly normalized factor but not a product of unit-wise factors. Eligibility conditioning must be shown separately to preserve the asserted law. The condition L≥hL\geq h is sufficient, not necessary. In the trap experiment of §7, each episode is tested as one unit, and its frozen episode-local policy draws each action from a law that depends only on that episode’s own state at least h=4h=4 steps before the action, with fresh randomization; treating the simulator’s pseudorandom draws as independent innovations, the design-law analysis therefore falls under (b), with no eligibility conditioning and a target mask that does not depend on the actions under the null. This does not cover the deliberately marginal resampler of the negative control (§7.2).

5 Synthetic validation

Before any real outcome was reopened, the registered pooled statistic passed through four layers of synthetic checks, each fixed before it was run: development simulations with known truth (M2a), calibration on the real command records with synthetic outcomes (M2b), a power pilot and an end-to-end rehearsal (M2c, M2e), and a sealed challenge built in a separate session after the method was frozen (M3). We report what each layer tested and, equally, what it could not have detected. A fifth check, a single-field rehearsal for M5, is described at the end. Full tables are in Appendix D.

5.1 Development simulations

The development grid crossed five design laws (renewal, bounded walk, Markov, clock-locked and shuffle) with linear, saturating and delayed outcome dynamics, for each of the four reference models, with 256 replicates per cell. It contained four null families—the stand-in construction of Proposition 6, sharp-null mutual spillover (an own-channel null), shared noise under the global null, and zero-entropy designs—and two alternatives built from the masked effects of Proposition 3.

Validity.

Across all designs, dynamics and models, the exact and MC e-value tests never rejected in the stand-in family (0/256 for the exact form and 0/256 for the MC form, in every cell), and rejected at most 5/256 under shared noise and 3/256 under sharp-null spillover. The batch randomization p-value at a single origin is a p-value test at level 0.050.05 with B=127B=127, so its attainable nominal rate is 6/1286/128, or 1212 of 256256 replicates. Across the 240 null cells of the grid (60 in each null family) it rejected in at most 20 of 256256 replicates, a count reached in 1 cell, under shared noise; 26 cells exceeded 1212. With this many cells, some counts above 1212 are expected from binomial variation alone. In the largest stand-in setting, with 512512 units, the four models rejected at rates from 4.3% to 6.6%, none significantly above the nominal rate (smallest one-sided binomial tail probability 0.096). Validity means a rejection rate at most α\alpha, not zero rejections; the e-value tests reject far less often than α\alpha because Markov’s inequality is conservative.

The stand-in construction.

In the stand-in family the replacement diagnostics reported an action effect in up to 246/256 (zero block), 249/256 (another unit’s block) and 236/256 (retraining without actions) replicates, although no action had any effect. In the largest setting of the construction every model’s zero-block and swap diagnostics reported an effect in every replicate (minima across models 256/256 for the zero block and 256/256 for the swap), while the e-value tests never rejected (0/256; Figure 4B). The diagnostics fail just as badly in zero-entropy designs, where the actions follow a deterministic schedule and the randomization test returns e≡1e\equiv 1 by construction: there they reported effects in up to 254/256 replicates. A randomization test that resamples from the marginal frequency of each action instead of the design law (B-marg) reported effects in up to 256/256 stand-in replicates, the same failure that §7 reproduces in the pixel world.

Power where the design allows little.

The masked alternatives were built to be hard: their effects are invisible to unit-wise marginal comparisons. The e-value tests rejected in at most 9/256 replicates for masked XOR effects and 97/256 for masked shared effects. We report this as a limitation, not a failure of validity; the sealed challenge reproduces it (§5.4).

5.2 Calibration with the real command records

Proposition 5 does not license tests under working laws whose distance from the true law is unknown, so the working laws were calibrated on the released command records themselves. Each replicate drew a fresh random subset of real command paths and fresh synthetic outcomes from a model satisfying the sharp null, so that the estimated size averages over whatever law generated the released commands while the test resamples from the working law. The pre-committed criterion required the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bound on size to be at most 0.060.06 in every primary cell. All 64 of 64 primary cells passed; the largest point false-positive rate was 0.40% and the largest upper bound 1.3%. One generator placed the stand-in construction on the real command records, with a slowly decaying response to past commands and strongly autocorrelated noise; there the test rejected in at most 0.40% of replicates, whereas retraining without actions and zero-block replacement reported effects in up to 92.8% and 91% of them.

5.3 Power pilot and end-to-end rehearsal

On the full M4 grid of origins, all 16 of 16 null cells passed the registered validity gate (largest upper bound 3.1%), and the four-model average had minimum power across cells of 100% at 10%10\% signal and 100% at 30%30\%. At 2%2\% signal, power for ERK at thirty minutes ranged from 4.5% to 71%, which the specification recorded as a limitation. An end-to-end rehearsal of the frozen pipeline on a simple synthetic generator rejected strongly (log⁡E=136\log E=136 at ten minutes).

Neither check could have revealed pooling amplification. The pilot gave each synthetic ERK field a single outcome trajectory, not hundreds of cells sharing one light program, and the rehearsal’s generator was simple enough for the fitted models to be nearly correctly specified. The pooled statistic therefore entered M4 without ever having been scored on many sites that share an action sequence under a misspecified model—precisely the setting in which it fails (§6). We regard this as the main gap in our pre-registration validation.

5.4 Sealed challenge

The sealed challenge was generated in a separate session after the method was frozen and registered, from generators the method author never saw, and scored with the frozen implementation; the analysis functions used were verified identical to those of M4. It comprised 11 families: new designs and dynamics, an omitted-history stand-in construction, spillover on a given graph, shared autoregressive outcome noise, masked XOR effects, a known approximate-law error and zero-entropy designs. Its frozen criteria were a size bound, power where the design permits it, and exact neutrality under zero entropy.

The pooled statistic registered for M4 rejected in 0/3400 null replicates (pooled upper bound 0.088%; largest per-family upper bound 1.5%). Zero-entropy cells returned ee and EE equal to one exactly. Of the 16 alternative cells whose exact design ceiling was at least 0.950.95, 15 reached the required power of 0.800.80. The exception was the masked XOR family, with 24/200 rejections (12%) against a ceiling of 100%. Its effects are sharp but masked marginally, as in the masked alternatives of the development grid (§5.1), which were also the hard case there. As in M2, the replacement diagnostics reported effects at high rates in null families (Figure 8). Two disclosures apply. The challenge’s designer had seen the source of the reference models and one correction to the challenge design. And none of its families was built around units with many sites sharing an action sequence (Appendix D lists them), so, like the pilot, it was not designed to reveal pooling amplification.

5.5 A single-field rehearsal for M5

Before the M5 plan was finalized, the Kish-tempered statistic was rehearsed on synthetic outcomes attached to one real training field’s command path, with the linear-Gaussian model only and the rejection threshold E≥40E\geq 40 of the draft plan, which then had two primary horizons. With the simple synthetic response the statistic rejected in every replicate at both horizons (for example 32/32 at ten minutes with field-wide shared noise). With the harder generator and field-wide shared noise it rejected in 27/32 replicates at ten minutes but only 2/32 at thirty minutes. The registered plan therefore made ten minutes the only primary horizon, with threshold E≥20E\geq 20; because E≥40E\geq 40 implies E≥20E\geq 20, these counts are lower bounds on the rehearsal’s rejections at the registered threshold.

6 Pooling amplification and its repair

The registered M4 analysis failed on its own positive controls (§8.2). This section reports how we diagnosed the failure and selected a repair, on synthetic outcomes attached to the ERK command records, and a pre-declared demonstration of the same failure in a pixel world model. Everything here is exploratory. The diagnosis and the selection used no test outcome, and the repaired statistic was then confirmed on a field that no one had opened (§8.4). A later exploratory study (§6.4) compared the repairs with statistics that estimate no factor, and its outcome fixed the primary statistic of a registered test on a published world model (§9).

6.1 Diagnosis on ERK-like synthetic data

We attached synthetic outcomes to the command records of the M4 test fields, with five hundred cells per field, and fitted the linear-Gaussian reference model exactly as in M4. Three findings located the failure.

First, the pooled score collapsed without any shared noise. With independent cell noise, its median log⁡E\log E at ten minutes was −-317 at 10%10\% signal and −-1680 at 30%30\%: a stronger effect made the evidence more negative, as (5) predicts when a misspecified model’s error along the contrast grows with the effect it misrepresents. These medians come from the diagnostic runs, with thirty-two replicates per cell; the selection grid of §6.2, with sixteen replicates per cell, gives similar values (Table 11).

Second, the oracle predictor rejected in every replicate (16/16 at ten minutes and 16/16 at thirty), and the pipeline remained valid under the null (0/64 rejections with mean ee 1.00027 on ERK commands, 0/64 with mean ee 0.99998 on CcaS commands). The oracle’s log⁡E\log E of 135 at ten minutes is a ceiling set by ties among resampled blocks—the generator responds only to the last action of the block—and not the design bound of Proposition 4.

Third, changing the pipeline one component at a time showed that a single step caused the collapse: summing the cells’ log scores and then normalizing once over the field’s design (rejections 8/8 before that step, 0/8 after it; Figure 2B). Adding field-wide shared noise to the simple rehearsal generator of §5.3 also collapsed the pooled score (median log⁡E\log E −-10,494 at ten minutes in the selection grid of §6.2): noise shared by all cells moves them in the direction of the contrast, so it amplifies in the same way as model error.

6.2 Selecting a repair

Before evaluating any candidate, we committed a protocol listing three repairs and a selection rule. The candidates were the Kish-tempered score (§3.4), a field-mean score that scores the field-average outcome under a Gaussian whose variance accounts for the within-field correlation, and a site-average that averages per-cell e-values; each kept the design law, the Monte Carlo bags and the aggregation of M4. The grid crossed two generators (the first at two signal levels), two levels of shared noise and both horizons, giving twelve alternative cells with sixteen replicates each, and two null cells with thirty-two replicates each. The rule was: (1) exclude a candidate with two or more null rejections in any null cell; (2) choose the highest minimum rejection rate across alternative cells; (3) break ties by the highest median log⁡E\log E in the hardest cell, the one with the lowest pooled rejection rate; (4) break remaining ties by simplicity, Kish first.

All three candidates rejected in every replicate of every alternative cell (minimum rates 100% for Kish tempering, 100% for the field mean and 100% for the site average) and in no null replicate (Kish tempering: 0/32 and 0/32 in the two null cells; the other candidates likewise, Appendix D). Step (2) therefore tied, and the selection fell to step (3). Because every cell tied on the pooled rejection rate, the “hardest cell” was not defined by the rule; the selection script took the first cell in grid order. That script was first committed together with the selection result, after the evaluation, so we cannot show that this detail was fixed in advance. In that cell the median log⁡E\log E was 131.53 for Kish tempering, 131.39 for the field mean and 83.60 for the site average. Across the twelve possible designations of the hardest cell, the rule would have selected Kish tempering in 9 of them, the field mean in 2 and the site average in 1; the Kish-minus-field-mean difference in median log⁡E\log E ranged from −-0.04 to 0.96. On this evidence Kish tempering and the field-mean score perform alike, both well ahead of the site average (Figure 2A). Kish tempering was registered for the confirmatory test; its registration describes the selection as following the pre-committed rule, and we correct that description here (Appendix D).

6.3 A pixel world model

To show the failure where machine-learning practice meets it, we ran a demonstration under a protocol frozen before any learned model was trained, with dated predictions committed before the main run. A Gaussian blob moves on an R×RR\times R frame; each action pushes it in one of four directions or leaves it, and a delayed restoring force adds memory. Frames carry independent pixel noise and one of three kinds of frame-level shared noise: none, an additive offset, or a multiplicative gain on the blob. Actions are drawn uniformly at random, so the design law is known exactly. Two learned models predict the frame four steps ahead from the last two frames and the action window, a convolutional network with action conditioning and a per-pixel ridge regression, and are compared with oracles that know the true dynamics. Each episode is one unit and its n=R2n=R^{2} pixels are its sites, from 6464 to 40964096; the effect size was calibrated on the oracle alone. Every statistic uses Monte Carlo e-values with B=127B=127 and the rejection rule E≥20E\geq 20, and reports the average of the two models.

The pooled score collapses as pixels are added, and the cause is misspecification.

Figure 1 shows the main grid. With no shared noise and the larger effect, the median log⁡E\log E of the pooled score fell from −-17.3 at 6464 pixels to −-6832 at 40964096, while the oracle’s rose from 79.0 to 157. The pattern was the same under offset and gain noise (pooled score at 40964096 pixels −-5996 and −-6567; oracle 155 and 157), and from 256256 pixels on the pooled score never rejected under any noise (0%). Because the oracle does not collapse under either form of shared noise, the collapse of the fitted models is due to their misspecification. Our protocol had predicted that the gain noise would make even the oracle collapse; it did not, because a multiplicative gain rescales the oracle’s evidence without changing its sign.

Kish tempering does not repair it here.

The pixel residuals of a misplaced blob take both signs, so their median pairwise correlation is nearly zero without shared noise or with gain noise (at most 0.000629 across cells), the Kish factor is close to one, and Kish tempering behaves like the pooled score: it rejected in 6.2% of episodes at 6464 pixels and in none from 256256 on. Under offset noise the residual correlation rose to between 0.159 and 0.182, and Kish tempering did reject, but for the wrong reason: the offset raises the residual correlation while being orthogonal to the action contrast, and at 40964096 pixels the resulting over-tempering cut its rejection rate to 43.8%. Kish tempering, the statistic registered for M5, therefore does not repair pooling amplification in the pixel world. The fractional-Kelly reference arm of §3.6, which bounds each factor below but keeps the pooled bet, rejected in 0% to 75% of episodes at the larger effect (Appendix G).

Contrast tempering restores power, not information.

Contrast tempering, declared in the protocol as an exploratory generalization, rejected in 81.2% to 100% of episodes across all noise conditions and frame sizes at the larger effect, against 100% for the oracle with the exact joint likelihood. Its median log⁡E\log E, however, stayed between 7.06 and 10.3 and did not grow with the number of pixels, far below the oracle: it removes the amplification but does not convert the additional pixels into additional evidence. At the smaller effect every learned statistic was weak (contrast tempering at most 25%). Section 6.4 shows that statistics estimating no factor matched these rejection rates, and §9 that contrast tempering did not carry over to a published world model.

The mechanism of §3.4 was visible directly (Figure 3). For the learned models in the main grid, the contrast design effect exceeded the Kish design effect in every row without shared noise or with gain noise (48/48) and fell below it in every offset row (24/24), as predicted before the main run. For the oracles, whose residuals are independent pixel noise, both design effects are close to one and their ordering carries no information (Appendix G).

Scope.

Every statistic was valid in every null cell. The demonstration uses one simulator family, two model classes and one training run per cell; compute limits reduced the episode length and the number of test episodes, so the intervals for alternative cells are wide (Appendix G). Contrast tempering has only this simulation evidence; on a published world model it did not repair pooling amplification (§9), and we do not recommend it.

6.4 Statistics that estimate no factor

Both repairs above estimate a tempering factor from validation residuals. We asked whether statistics that need no such estimate do as well: the tempering mixture M over a fixed grid of thirteen factors, validation-tuned tempering V, and the rank e-values R and R1/2 (§3.5). Before any of them was computed we committed a protocol with dated predictions and mechanical decision rules. We then recomputed every existing statistic from the saved models, episodes and seeds of the pixel demonstration and of the selection grid of §6.2, on a different machine, and computed the new statistics on the same draws. The recomputation reproduced every rejection decision of the original runs. Its reproduction criterion, as first written, used a relative tolerance that is ill-posed for values near zero; we amended it before any new statistic was computed (Appendix H). This study is exploratory.

Table 2 gives the results. At the larger effect the mixture and validation tuning matched contrast tempering, and the mixture also rejected where Kish tempering had failed. The pre-registered rule therefore returned outcome 1: a statistic that estimates no factor matched contrast tempering in the pixel world and Kish tempering on ERK-like data. Validation tuning matched contrast tempering, so the contrast formula added nothing over a temperature chosen on validation data. At the smaller effect the mixture was weaker than contrast tempering and validation tuning, though not than Kish tempering. Averaging can reduce log evidence relative to the best grid member by up to log⁡13≈2.56\log 13\approx 2.56, which can matter near a rejection threshold; the bound alone does not determine these observed differences. The rank e-value R failed, against our dated prediction. On the ERK-like grid its largest count in any cell was 0 of sixteen replicates, consistent with the expected price per factor that a rank calibrator pays when evidence is spread over thousands of weakly informative factors (Proposition 11, stated for untied scores); R1/2, a secondary arm, did well in the pixel world but likewise failed on ERK-like data (largest count 2 of sixteen). No new statistic rejected more than 1 of the episodes of any null cell. On the strength of this study the mixture became the primary statistic of the registered test in §9.

6.5 A regime map (exploratory)

Section 6.4 compared the statistics in two settings. To see where each one works, we ran a simulator in which the relevant quantities can be set directly, under a protocol committed before any statistic was computed (Appendix K). A unit has 200 origins, and recorded actions are drawn uniformly from four. The executed action equals the recorded one with probability pp and is otherwise an independent draw. Each of nn sites responds to the executed action through a fixed pattern, plus shared noise of variance ρ\rho that moves the sites the way an action would, plus independent noise. The model predicts the response to the recorded action, with an error along the action contrast that is a fraction δ\delta of the effect and is shared by all sites; it assumes that the recorded action was executed. The grid crossed n∈{16,256,4096}n\in\{16,256,4096\}, ρ∈{0,0.05}\rho\in\{0,0.05\}, δ∈{0,0.25,0.5}\delta\in\{0,0.25,0.5\}, p∈{1,0.5,0.2}p\in\{1,0.5,0.2\} and three effect sizes calibrated on the oracle alone, with 32 test units in each of the 162 alternative cells and 64 in each of the 18 null cells.

The pooled score behaved as §3.3 predicts. With δ=0\delta=0 and p≤0.5p\leq 0.5 it collapsed at 4096 sites in all 12 such cells: when the recorded action is not always executed, a model that assumes it was is misspecified along the contrast even if its response pattern is exact. Kish tempering did no better than the pooled score, with mean rejection rates of 0.222 and 0.221 over the alternative cells; contrast tempering reached 0.496. Validation tuning had the highest mean rate, 0.635, followed by the weighted mixtures (0.625, 0.609 and 0.588 for w=3/4,1/2,1/4w=3/4,1/2,1/4) and the uniform mixture (0.560). In the 98 cells of the simulator and of the saved pixel runs in which some candidate rejected in at least 80

The protocol’s mechanical rule chose the primary statistic of the next registered test among M, W(1/4), W(1/2), W(3/4) and V. It selected V, which tied with W(3/4) within the rule’s tolerance and won on mean rate. The simulator could not test V on ERK-like data, because the saved ERK-like runs lack the validation residuals V needs. Section 8.6 tests V on the real ERK test fields, where it collapsed. For that reason the next registered test used W(3/4) instead of V, a departure from the rule that was recorded in the registered protocol before any of that test’s data existed (§10.1).

7 The stand-in trap

Section 2.4 and Proposition 6 describe how a predictor can make future actions look effective when they are not. The development simulations and the calibration on real command records showed the trap on biological designs (§5). Here we build it into the pixel world, where every quantity is known, and test what the randomization test needs in order to avoid it.

7.1 A pixel world with a stand-in

The logging policy now depends on state the model cannot see: with probability 0.60.6 it chooses the action that points from the blob’s position six steps earlier toward the centre of the frame, and each other action with probability 0.10.1. The model sees only the last two frames, so the future actions carry information about an earlier position that the restoring force still acts on. The actions themselves have no effect. We used 256256-pixel frames, training sets of 1616, 6464 and 256256 episodes, and either no shared noise or gain noise. The randomization test resamples each future action from the logging policy given the full logged state, which the design records.

The replacement diagnostics—retraining without actions, setting the actions to zero, and shuffling the action windows across origins within an episode—reported an action effect in most test episodes (Figure 4A): for the convolutional model in 90.6% to 100% of them, and for the ridge model in 64.1% to 100%, across diagnostics, training sizes and noise conditions. With the design-law resampler the randomization test never rejected: the Kish-tempered statistic rejected in 0% of episodes in every cell, and the contrast-tempered statistic plotted in Figure 4A in none for the two-model average (§7.2). The experiment does not show the growth of the diagnostics’ confidence with data that Proposition 6 describes: with the smallest training set, the convolutional model’s diagnostics already reported effects in at least 90.6% of episodes, leaving no room to grow. That property rests on the proposition and on the development simulations (§5.1).

7.2 The resampler must condition on the design state

The protocol included a negative control: the Kish-tempered statistic with a deliberately wrong resampler that draws each action from its marginal frequency in the training episodes, ignoring the logged state. It was expected to reject often. It never rejected (0/64 episodes in every cell), and the pre-declared criterion for the negative control was not met. The result is uninformative rather than reassuring: without shared noise or with gain noise, Kish tempering coincides with the pooled score at this frame size, and the pooled score has no power there (§6.3). A statistic whose log⁡E\log E is driven far below zero by amplification cannot reveal that a resampler is invalid.

After seeing this result we added one post hoc analysis, declared in a dated note committed before any of its e-values were computed: the same wrong resampler with the contrast-tempered statistic, which does have power, on the sealed episodes, frozen models and frozen tempering factors of the six trap cells. The wrong resampler rejected in 98.4% to 100% of episodes for the two-model average (92.2% to 100% for the individual models). With the correct resampler, whose results were read from the sealed records rather than recomputed, the same statistic never rejected for the two-model average (0/64 episodes in every cell); one single-model cell had 1/64. The wrong resampler rejected more often in 18/18 comparisons. This analysis is post hoc and exploratory; it does not replace the frozen negative control, whose criterion remains unmet.

Two lessons follow. First, the conditioning in Assumption 1 is not a technicality: a resampler that ignores part of the state the design used is far from the design law in total variation, nothing in Proposition 5 protects it, and it reproduces the false effect that the replacement diagnostics report. Second, a negative control needs a statistic with power; pooling amplification can hide invalidity as easily as it hides an effect.

7.3 Summary across settings

The same three-way pattern appears in every setting we examined. Replacement diagnostics report effects at high rates when there is none: in the development simulations, on real command records with synthetic outcomes, in the sealed challenge, and in the pixel world. A randomization test that resamples from the design law, conditioning on the full state the design used, keeps its error rate. A randomization test that resamples from a simpler law loses that guarantee and reproduces the diagnostics’ error. On the real ERK data the diagnostics reported an effect that is biologically established, so we do not count those reports as instances of the trap (§8.2).

8 Real data

The real-data evidence has three stages, each with a different evidential status. M4 is the registered analysis of two previously analyzed datasets. X is a single exploratory application of the repaired statistic to the M4 test fields. M5 is a registered confirmatory test of the repaired statistic on a field that no one involved had opened. Appendix E gives registration identifiers, hashes and the time-ordering of every data access; Appendix D lists every deviation and disclosure.

8.1 Data, units and design laws

ERK.

In the ERK experiment (Nałęcz-Jawecki et al., 2023), with data released as Nałęcz-Jawecki et al. (2022), each microscope field receives one light program, a sequence of pulses whose inter-pulse intervals were randomized by the acquisition protocol, and the field’s hundreds of cells are recorded under that common program. The field is therefore the assignment unit and its cells are sites; the spillover graph between fields is empty, so the primary null is H0GH_{0}^{G}. The working design law, V3, shuffles the inter-pulse intervals uniformly within interval groups, conditionally on the elapsed interval at the origin, and preserves the protocol’s rest segment; two variants, V1 and V2, serve as sensitivity laws. Fields run under a binary policy are deterministic and contribute e≡1e\equiv 1. The reference models were trained on four minimum-gap fields from the first replicate and tested on four minimum-gap fields from the second replicate and five ordinary-interval fields.

CcaS/CcaR.

In the CcaS/CcaR experiment (Lugagne et al., 2024), with data and trained models released as Lugagne et al. (2023), each cell lineage receives its own light program from a random walk, bounded in the released acquisition code, so each lineage is a unit with a single site. The working law, D1, is the generator in the released acquisition code delayed by one step, consistent with a shift at data export; the delay was found after the first design-law checks failed (Appendix C). Every CcaS rejection below is conditional on D1. Lineages that follow one of two duplicated fixed templates have zero design entropy and contribute e≡1e\equiv 1; the remaining lineages are tested under the design law conditioned on avoiding both templates (Proposition 2(b)), which keeps the test exact. In addition to the four reference models, we test the published model of Lugagne et al. (2024) with its released preprocessing, after replacing its neighbour-exposure input by the lagged, admissible version (§2.3).

Models and prior use.

The four reference models (linear-Gaussian, GRU, small Transformer and gradient boosting) are additive: an own-history branch plus an action branch fitted to its residual. They were trained on training-unit outcomes only and frozen by hash before any test outcome was opened; their Gaussian variances come from held-out validation data. Both datasets were analyzed earlier in our BioWM-Eval study (Appendix A); M4 is therefore a re-analysis, not a blind test, although every M4 setting was fixed on synthetic data and command records before the outcomes were reopened.

8.2 M4: the registered analysis

M4 tests five prespecified hypotheses with the pooled statistic (Table 3): ERK at horizons of ten and thirty minutes, registered as positive controls because optogenetic stimulation is known to drive ERK activity; CcaS at one and six five-minute steps with the four-model average; and CcaS at twelve steps with the published model. A slot is rejected iff E≥100E\geq 100, the e-Bonferroni rule for five hypotheses at family level 0.050.05.

Neither positive control was rejected, and the failure was not marginal: every reference model gave a strongly negative log⁡E\log E for ERK (from −-17,989 to −-2973), and so did both sensitivity laws. By the interpretation registered with M4, a strongly negative log⁡E\log E for a model means that its predictions under the observed actions scored worse than its predictions averaged over the design; it is not evidence against an effect. A dated note written after we had read the M4 report fixes further interpretation rules; it was written post hoc, and its rules only restrict what may be claimed (Appendix D). Section 6 shows that the failure is pooling amplification: the ERK score sums hundreds of cells that share one action sequence.

Both CcaS hypotheses at the longer horizons were rejected. Restricting the published model to lineages whose lagged exposure could be verified from commands gives log⁡E=16,771\log E=16{,}771. A second sensitivity analysis that uses the raw neighbour exposure with singleton averaging gives 3.02; it changes both the exposure alignment and the aggregation, is not a valid test, and is reported descriptively only. The secondary own-channel analysis at six steps gives log⁡E\log E from 617 to 1338 across models, but its eligibility bound is vacuous (Proposition 2(a)), so it is descriptive.

Two secondary results bear on the diagnosis. The batch randomization p-value at a single prespecified origin gave per-model values from 1/128 to 2/128 for ERK at thirty minutes and 12/128 for every model at ten minutes (unadjusted, secondary). A rank-based p-value depends only on where the observed score ranks among the design draws, not on the size of the score differences, so it does not suffer from the over-aggressive betting that drives pooling amplification. The contrast with the e-value product is consistent with the diagnosis; but the registered interface covers such p-values only at one common origin, whereas e-values combine evidence across all origins. Second, the replacement diagnostics reported an ERK action effect, with risk differences from 14.6% to 46.3%. The ERK effect is biologically real, so these are most likely true positives and we do not use them as examples of the stand-in trap. For CcaS at one step the same diagnostics reported effects of magnitude 2.9×10−82.9\times 10^{-8} to 2.9×10−42.9\times 10^{-4} while the randomization test did not reject; the truth there is unknown, so this is descriptive only.

8.3 X: an exploratory check on the M4 test fields

After diagnosing the failure (§6), we selected the Kish-tempered statistic on synthetic data and applied it once, with every parameter fixed on training data, to the nine ERK test fields of M4. We call this analysis X. It is exploratory: the fields had been opened in M4, and the analysis was run because the pooled statistic had failed there. No test outcome was used to choose the statistic or its parameters. The four-model log⁡E\log E was 349 at ten minutes and 218 at thirty minutes, against −-9576 and −-2975 for the pooled statistic on the same data; the individual models ranged from 185 to 350. The exact-form design bound of Proposition 4 for these fields is 925 at both horizons, and X reached 37.7% and 23.5% of it on the log scale. Because X used Monte Carlo e-values, this is a descriptive comparison rather than a ceiling; the corresponding Monte Carlo bound of Proposition 4(a), computed in the M5 registration package from the frozen Monte Carlo bags, is 914 at ten minutes and 848 at thirty. The ratios are not power estimates. These values are reported descriptively: X was prompted by outcomes already opened in M4, and no formal error guarantee is claimed for it.

8.4 M5: a confirmatory test on an unopened field

Design.

M5 tests the repaired statistic on one ERK field, a minimum-gap field with thirty-minute minimum intervals from the first replicate. It had been excluded from M4 by the scope of the registered sample (minimum gaps of ten to twenty-five minutes, two replicates), not for data quality. None of our projects had opened it, and before registration the first author recorded a statement that he had never opened, previewed or plotted its outcomes (Appendix E). The analysis plan was committed before X was run and was not changed afterwards (its committed and registered bytes are identical). It was registered before the data were obtained, in a new registration linked to the M4 registration, together with a disclosure that the X results were available when the plan was finalized. The only primary hypothesis is H0GH_{0}^{G} at ten minutes, rejected iff E≥20E\geq 20; thirty minutes is computed and reported descriptively only. The registered plan chose this horizon before any M5 data were obtained, because a single-field rehearsal had shown weak power at thirty minutes under shared noise (§5). The statistic is the Kish-tempered score with all parameters frozen on the training fields, the working law V3, and Monte Carlo e-values with B=127B=127.

Command-law gate.

Before any outcome statistic was computed, a registered gate checked the reconstructed command series alone: that commands were shared by all cells, that every non-rest inter-pulse interval was at least thirty minutes (the minimum was 31 minutes), that the frozen parser found the rest segment (at interval rank 15), and that the exchangeability diagnostics used for the M4 fields did not flag the interval sequence (p=0.27p=0.27, 0.370.37 and 0.560.56, against the inherited per-statistic threshold 0.01/390.01/39). The gate passed.

Result.

The primary hypothesis was rejected (Figure 5): the four-model log⁡E\log E at ten minutes was 23.1, that is E≈1.1×1010E\approx 1.1\times 10^{10}. All four models agreed (23.0, 23.0, 22.5 and 23.7). The field had 500 cells and 1581 origins; 560,409 cell–origin pairs contributed, 230,091 were excluded by the observation mask, and 1083 factors had zero design entropy. The exact-form design bound is 51.7, and the statistic reached 44.7% of it on the log scale, a descriptive comparison as for X. At thirty minutes the descriptive log⁡E\log E was 19.1 (models from 17.0 to 19.9); it carries no confirmatory decision.

What M5 shows.

Conditional on the registered design, observation-process and frozen-training assumptions, with the working law V3, the rejection is evidence against the sharp null H0GH_{0}^{G} on a new field: M5 detects the known ERK action effect with the repaired statistic. It does not estimate the size of the effect, it says nothing about power for CcaS or other systems, and it does not validate the forecast gains reported in BioWM-Eval, which answer a different question with a with-versus-without-actions comparison of the kind §7 shows can be inflated. The evidence is narrow: one field, one dataset, one horizon. The field’s thirty-minute intervals lie outside the training range of ten to twenty-five minutes, which may reduce power; the exact acquisition law for this field is unverified, so validity is conditional on V3; and the gate’s threshold, inherited from the multi-field M1 analysis, is lenient for a single field.

8.5 Kish versus contrast tempering on the ERK training fields

To ask whether the registered Kish factor is a reasonable choice on ERK, we compared it with the contrast factor of §3.4 on the training fields’ validation cells. This diagnostic is exploratory and descriptive: it used training outcomes only, computed no e-value, and touched no test field; its reading rule was fixed before the data were accessed. Expressing the contrast factor as an implied correlation ρc\rho_{c}, the pooled ratio ρc/ρ^\rho_{c}/\hat{\rho} ranged from 0.554 to 0.818 across models at ten minutes and from 0.574 to 0.828 at thirty minutes. All values fall inside the pre-declared band from 0.50.5 to 22, so by the pre-declared reading Kish tempering is approximately adequate on ERK; all are below one, so Kish tempering over-tempers somewhat and is conservative there. Individual fields gave ratios from 0.41 to 1.27; Appendix F lists every field.

Two qualifications follow from Proposition 7. Because the action branch of the ERK reference models predicts the same response for every cell of a field, the contrast is shared across cells and the contrast factor has the form of Proposition 7: a Kish factor with a contrast-weighted residual correlation, at an effective cell count since counts vary across origins. The agreement is therefore partly structural, and the diagnostic is not an independent validation of the Kish rule. And the gap is not only a matter of median versus mean: against the mean pairwise residual correlation the ratio at ten minutes was still between 0.598 and 0.854, so contrast weighting itself lowers the effective correlation; we did not decompose the remainder further. The diagnostic used the validation cells of each training field, fewer than the cells of a test field, so comparisons at test-field size assume that correlations do not change with the number of cells. We did not compute contrast-tempered e-values on the M5 field, and we make no claim about what they would have been.

8.6 Validation tuning on the ERK test fields (exploratory)

Validation tuning and the mixtures had no ERK entry in §6.4, because the saved ERK-like runs lack the validation quantities they need. We therefore computed them on the nine ERK test fields of M4, as a second exploratory analysis after X, under a protocol committed before the fields were reopened (Appendix K). Everything was as in X—the models, the design law V3 and X’s frozen Monte Carlo bags—except that each model’s factor for V was chosen on the validation cells of the four training fields, with 31 design draws per origin. A reproduction gate first recomputed the four-model log EE of the pooled statistic in M4 and of the Kish-tempered statistic in X; both matched.

Validation tuning collapsed (Table 4). Its four-model log EE was 210 at ten minutes, with two of the four models strongly negative (−1420-1420 and −979-979), and −101-101 at thirty minutes, with all four models negative. The uniform mixture gave 347 and 218, W(3/4) 345 and 217, and Kish tempering 349 and 218 as in X; the mixture was within log⁡15\log 15 of the best fixed grid member at both horizons, as Proposition 10 requires. The factor chosen on the training fields was 1/32 to 1/4, whereas the per-origin Kish factor on the test fields was about 0.008 to 0.04. One reading is that a factor tuned on the training fields’ validation cells, which are fewer than the cells of a test field, is too large for the test fields; this reading is post hoc. The analysis is exploratory for the same reasons as X: the fields had been opened, and no error guarantee is claimed for it.

These fields cannot serve a confirmatory test of the mixture, and no other field of this dataset can either: an inventory of the released ERK data, using archive metadata and our own records only, found no randomized field that we could certify as never opened by any of our projects (Appendix K). A registered biological test of the mixture therefore needs new data.

9 A published world model

Every model in the preceding sections was built by us. If pooling amplification is a property of pooled scores and not of our models, it should appear on a world model trained by others, and the statistic chosen in §6.4 should repair it there. We tested both claims in a registered confirmatory study on DIAMOND (Alonso et al., 2024), a diffusion world model for Atari games whose authors released trained checkpoints. We neither trained nor modified the models.

9.1 Design

Models and environment.

We used the released checkpoints for Boxing, Pong and Breakout at a fixed revision, with their hashes recorded before registration (Appendix I). The Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013), an interface to the Stella Atari 2600 emulator, was configured exactly as for DIAMOND’s training: four frames per action, the maximum of the last two frames, 64×6464\times 64 RGB frames, no sticky actions and the minimal action sets of 1818, 66 and 44 actions. The model predicts the next frame from the last four frames and actions with a three-step sampler; at each origin one noise image was drawn and shared by every candidate action, so the prediction is a fixed function of the candidate. The candidate block is the next action (h=1h=1), and the sites are the n=64⋅64⋅3=12,288n=64\cdot 64\cdot 3=12{,}288 pixel channels. The score is the Gaussian log density of the observed next frame around the predicted one, with per-site variances estimated on validation units and floored at the square of one intensity step.

Two conditions.

In the ACTIVE condition the emulator executed the recorded action, drawn uniformly at random, so actions matter. In the NULL condition the recorded labels were drawn the same way but the emulator executed an independent random sequence, so the labels have no effect on any frame and the null holds exactly. A unit is one segment of up to 500500 agent steps from a reset. Each game and condition had 1616 validation units; there were 3232 ACTIVE and 6464 NULL test units per game.

Statistics and criteria.

The primary statistic was the tempering mixture over fifteen factors, the grid reaching 1/n1/n (§3.5). The pooled score, Kish and contrast tempering, validation-tuned tempering, the thirteen-value mixture and the two rank e-values were secondary. Every statistic used the same Monte Carlo bags (B=127B=127), rejected at E≥20E\geq 20, and took its factors from the validation units of its own game and condition. The registered criteria, per game, were: validity, each statistic rejecting in at most 22 of the 6464 NULL units; collapse, a median pooled log⁡E\log E below zero in the ACTIVE units; and repair, the mixture rejecting in at least 2424 of the 3232 ACTIVE units. Overall confirmation required validity in all three games and both collapse and repair in at least two. Five dated predictions were registered with the criteria.

Registration and seeds.

The protocol, the identity of the frozen analysis code and a note on its dates were registered on OSF (ctfxv) before any confirmatory unit existed. The confirmatory seeds were derived from the first round of a public randomness beacon (League of Entropy, 2026) scheduled at least two minutes after the start of the minute in which OSF recorded the registration, so no unit could have been generated earlier. A pilot on separate seeds had run the full pipeline under NULL only; under ACTIVE it computed predictions and validation quantities but no e-value. Two integrity checks of the frozen code stopped the confirmatory run before any ACTIVE test unit was generated: a field-name collision in the access log, and a storage tolerance tighter than float32 rounding. Each was fixed by a dated deviation published on OSF before the run resumed with the same seeds, and every regenerated unit was identical, array by array, to its earlier copy (Appendix I).

9.2 Results

Table 5 gives the results. Pooling amplification appeared on the published models: although actions visibly move the player, paddle or ball, the pooled score rejected in 0 of the 9696 ACTIVE units, with median log⁡E\log E between −-222,582 and −-5408 across games. Tempering by an estimated factor did not prevent it: Kish tempering rejected in 0 and contrast tempering in 1 of the 9696 units, with medians from −-2698 to −-383 and from −-4012 to −-95.3. The mixture rejected in 96 of the 9696 units, with medians from 126 to 455; validation tuning, the thirteen-value mixture and both rank e-values did as well. Under the exact null the eight statistics made 0 rejections in 8×1928\times 192 tests, and the mixture’s median log⁡E\log E stayed between −-2.79 and −-1.35, comparable in magnitude to log⁡15≈2.71\log 15\approx 2.71, the largest log-e loss relative to the best member of the fifteen-factor grid (Proposition 10), although the proposition does not assert a null loss of that size.

All three criteria held in all three games, so the study confirmed its claim. Of the five predictions, 4 held. The one that failed was ours about ranks: we predicted that the rank e-value would reject less often than the mixture in at least two games, and it matched the mixture in all three. The replacement diagnostic reported an action effect in 96 of the 9696 ACTIVE units and in 5 of the 192192 NULL units; because the NULL labels are independent of everything the model sees, this design produces no stand-in effect, and the trap of §7 is not tested here.

The estimated factors were an order of magnitude or more above the factor selected on validation data. Across games, λK\lambda^{\mathrm{K}} ranged from 0.0181 to 0.320 and λc\lambda^{\mathrm{c}} from 0.0241 to 0.0773, whereas λV\lambda^{\mathrm{V}} was 0.00195 to 0.00391; the contrast factor exceeded it by a factor of 12.3 to 19.8. With predictions, residuals and contrasts held fixed, both estimated factors are invariant under a common multiplier of all site precisions, whereas for unfloored Gaussian scores the tempered log-e curve shifts by the inverse multiplier along the temperature axis (Proposition 9). This is consistent with a possible mechanism for the failure; it is a descriptive, post hoc reading and not a test (Appendix I gives the saved score bags it rests on).

9.3 What this shows

On world models that we did not build, the pooled design-based test collapsed although actions mattered, tempering by factors estimated from residuals did not prevent the collapse, and a mixture fixed in advance restored power while every statistic kept its error rate under an exact null. The study does not show that DIAMOND predicts the consequences of actions correctly: a rejection is evidence that the recorded actions affect the frames, read through the model’s predictions, not a validation of those predictions. The action effects in these games are strong, so the study says little about power for weak effects, where the mixture was weaker than contrast tempering in the pixel world (§6.4). It covers one model family, three games and a horizon of one step. Section 10 extends the test to two further model families.

9.4 Score rule and sampling noise (exploratory)

Two objections to §9.2 can be checked on the saved data: that the collapse is an artifact of the per-pixel Gaussian score, and that a single sampled prediction is too noisy. Both studies below are exploratory, under protocols committed before they were run (Appendix K).

Score rule.

We rescored every saved DIAMOND unit under ten alternative score rules, with predictions, observations and bags unchanged: two higher variance floors, (8/255)2(8/255)^{2} and (32/255)2(32/255)^{2}; one common variance for all sites; Student-t (ν=3\nu=3) and Laplace densities; averages over blocks of 2×\times2, 4×\times4 and 8×\times8 pixels; a random projection to 256 dimensions; and a joint Gaussian whose covariance is a rank-16 principal-component model of the validation residuals plus a diagonal. A reproduction gate first recovered every rejection decision of the registered run exactly. Under every rule, no statistic rejected in any of the 64 NULL units of any game, and the mixture rejected in all 32 ACTIVE units of every game. The pooled score collapsed under every rule in at least two of the three games, including under the joint Gaussian (median log EE −366,580-366{,}580, −66,379-66{,}379 and −4324-4324). Coarser scores weakened the collapse: with 8×\times8 blocks, 192 sites instead of 12,288, the median pooled log EE was −6656-6656 in Boxing, −77-77 in Pong and 67 in Breakout, against −222,582-222{,}582, −21,805-21{,}805 and −5408-5408 per pixel. Kish tempering reached 24 of 32 units in 1 of the 27 game–rule pairs in which it was defined. Contrast tempering depended on the rule: it reached 24 of 32 units in Pong or Breakout under the higher floors and the coarser blocks, and in Boxing only under the random projection.

Sampling noise.

DIAMOND samples its prediction, and the registered test used one sample per origin. We regenerated all 288 units of the three games with predictions averaged over four samples, after a reproduction gate had recovered a registered unit bit for bit. The collapse was unchanged: the median pooled log EE of the ACTIVE units was −220,241-220{,}241, −22,354-22{,}354 and −5553-5553, against −222,582-222{,}582, −21,805-21{,}805 and −5408-5408 with one sample. Kish and contrast tempering again rejected in 0 of 32 units in every game; validation tuning, the mixture and both rank e-values rejected in all 32; under the null every statistic rejected in 0 of 32 units. The factor chosen on validation data was 0.002 to 0.004, against Kish factors of 0.018 to 0.32.

10 Two further published world models

Section 9 covers one model family. We registered a second confirmatory test on two families that differ from DIAMOND, and from each other, in how they predict and how they can be scored: IRIS (Micheli et al., 2023), which compresses each frame into 16 discrete tokens and predicts the next frame’s tokens with an autoregressive Transformer, and TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024), which predicts in a learned latent space and has no decoder. Both were trained and released by their authors; we neither trained nor modified them.

10.1 Design

Models and environments.

For IRIS we used the released checkpoints of all 26 games of its benchmark, none excluded, with IRIS’s own preprocessing: four frames per action, the maximum of the last two frames, 64 ×\times 64 RGB frames, no sticky actions and minimal action sets. For TD-MPC2 we used released single-task checkpoints for three DeepMind Control Suite tasks (Tassa et al., 2018)—cartpole-balance, reacher-easy and walker-walk—and three MyoSuite tasks (Caggiano et al., 2022)—myo-pose, myo-reach and myo-obj-hold. Code revisions and checkpoint hashes, and one wrapper patch that changes no dynamics, were frozen before registration (Appendix J).

Scores.

For IRIS, the primary score is the model’s own log-likelihood of the 16 tokens of the observed next frame, computed by teacher forcing. It is a joint likelihood over the tokens, not a sum of independent site scores. As a secondary score in Boxing, Pong and Breakout, we decoded a sampled next frame and scored it with the per-pixel Gaussian of §9, over 12,288 sites. For TD-MPC2, which has no decoder, the score is a Gaussian on the 512 coordinates of the predicted next latent state, centred on the encoding of the observed next observation, with per-coordinate variances from validation units. The candidate block is the next action (h=1h=1) throughout.

Conditions.

Recorded labels were drawn uniformly at random. In an ACTIVE condition with execution probability pp, the executed action was the recorded label with probability pp and otherwise an independent uniform draw; p=1p=1 is full execution. In the NULL condition the executed actions were drawn independently of the labels, so the null holds exactly. Every game and task had p=1p=1 and NULL; Boxing, Pong, Breakout and the six control tasks also had p=0.5p=0.5, 0.2 and 0.05. Partial execution makes the action effect intermittent: the model assumes the recorded action was executed, so it is misspecified along the action contrast even where its dynamics are right. Each game or task and condition had 16 validation units and 32 test units, 64 under NULL. A unit is one segment of up to 500 steps from a reset, and of up to 100 or 75 steps for the MyoSuite tasks.

Primary statistic.

The primary statistic was the validation-weighted mixture W(3/4) of §3.5. The regime map’s rule had selected V (§6.5), but V collapsed on the ERK test fields (§8.6). Before any data of this test existed, we therefore registered W(3/4), which keeps most of V’s power when V’s factor is right and the mixture’s protection when it is wrong. The pooled score, Kish and contrast tempering (Gaussian scores only), V, M, M13, W(1/4), W(1/2) and both rank e-values were secondary. All statistics used the same bags (B=127B=127), took their factors from the validation units of their own game or task and condition, and rejected at E≥20E\geq 20.

Criteria and predictions.

For each primary arm—IRIS tokens and TD-MPC2—the registered criteria per game or task were validity, every statistic rejecting in at most 2 of the 64 NULL units, and power, W(3/4) rejecting in at least 24 of the 32 units at p=1p=1. An arm was confirmed if validity held in every game or task and power held in at least 18 of the 26 games, or in at least 4 of the 6 tasks. Eight dated predictions were registered with the criteria.

Registration, seeds and deviations.

The protocol and the identity of the frozen code were registered on OSF (j75g2) on 9 November 2026. As in §9, the seeds were derived from the first beacon round scheduled at least two minutes after the start of the minute in which OSF recorded the registration. A pilot on separate seeds had run the full pipeline under NULL only; under ACTIVE it computed predictions and validation quantities but no e-value. The confirmatory run generated all 5392 units once. Its last step, writing the decision file, failed on a data-type error in the JSON writer. A dated deviation changed only that conversion and wrote the decision from the stored, hashed results, and an independent script that does not use the frozen code reproduced every decision value. An earlier attempt had stopped before generating anything, because of an error in our run instruction, not in the protocol (Appendix J).

10.2 Results

Table 6 summarizes the results; Appendix J gives every game, task and condition.

Validity.

In the two primary arms the statistics made 4 rejections in 19,200 NULL tests, none of them by the primary statistic. No statistic rejected in more than 1 of the 64 NULL units of any game or task, so validity held everywhere. The secondary pixel score made 0 rejections in 2112 NULL tests.

Power.

W(3/4) rejected in at least 24 of 32 units at p=1p=1 in 24 of the 26 IRIS games and in all six TD-MPC2 tasks, so both arms were confirmed. It missed in BankHeist (16 of 32) and UpNDown (8 of 32), where no statistic reached the bar; validation tuning had 19 and 9.

The model’s own likelihood.

We had predicted, with probability 0.5, that the pooled token score would collapse at p=1p=1 in at least two of Boxing, Pong and Breakout. It collapsed in none of the three (median log EE 144, 428 and 121). It collapsed in all three once execution was partial (at p=0.5p=0.5: −3258-3258, −2615-2615 and −617-617). The protocol had fixed this outcome as meaning that amplification needs misspecification along the action contrast, and that a proper likelihood does not prevent it once the action model is wrong. Across all 26 games, which the prediction did not cover, the pooled token score had a negative median log EE at p=1p=1 in 14 and reached 24 of 32 units in 10. The factor chosen on validation data for tokens was between 1/16 and 1 across the 26 games, with median 1/4; in the three games scored both ways it was 1/4 to 1/2 for tokens and 1/1024 to 1/256 for decoded pixels. The model’s own likelihood needs far less tempering than an independent pixel score, but the factor chosen was below 1 in 25 of the 26 games.

Pixels and latents.

On the decoded pixels, the pattern of §9 recurred on a second model family: the pooled score and Kish tempering rejected in 0 of 96 units, contrast tempering in 20, and V, M and W(3/4) in 96. On TD-MPC2’s latent score, the pooled score reached the power bar in 1 of 6 tasks, Kish tempering in 2 and contrast tempering in 4. In reacher-easy and walker-walk the Kish factor was 1 in the NULL and partial-execution conditions—the residuals showed no correlation to correct for—while the factor chosen on validation data was between 6×10−56\times 10^{-5} and 8×10−38\times 10^{-3}.

Partial execution.

As execution became rarer, the pooled score failed first (Figure 7). At p=0.5p=0.5 it rejected in 0 of 32 units in all nine sets, while W(3/4) reached 24 of 32 in seven. At p=0.2p=0.2 W(3/4) reached the bar in four sets, and at p=0.05p=0.05 no statistic did in any set. W(3/4) rejected in more units than the pooled score at p=0.2p=0.2 in eight of the nine sets.

Of the eight dated predictions, seven held; the one that failed is the prediction about the token likelihood above. The replacement diagnostic reported an effect in 1 to 7 of the 64 NULL units of each game or task, and in most units at p=1p=1; as in §9, the NULL labels are independent of everything the model sees, so this design produces no stand-in effect.

10.3 What this shows

On two further model families and three kinds of score, the registered mixture kept its error rate under exact nulls and, at full execution, reached the power bar wherever any statistic did. Pooling amplification was not confined to Gaussian pixel scores: it appeared on a latent score and, in more than half of the games, on a model’s own token likelihood, although there much less tempering was needed. Factors estimated from residuals failed again; on two control tasks the Kish factor saw nothing to correct. The study does not validate the counterfactual predictions of these models: a rejection says that the recorded actions affect the observations, read through the model. It covers simulators with random actions and a horizon of one step, and weak effects only through partial execution, where every statistic had lost its power by p=0.05p=0.05.

11 Discussion and limitations

Across settings.

Table 7 collects every setting in which we compared the tempering statistics. Each statistic that relies on one factor collapsed—its median log e-value fell far below zero while another valid statistic rejected in most units—in at least one setting: the pooled score nearly everywhere; Kish tempering in the pixel world, on DIAMOND, on IRIS’s decoded pixels and on four TD-MPC2 tasks; contrast tempering on DIAMOND, on IRIS’s decoded pixels and on two TD-MPC2 tasks; and validation tuning on the ERK test fields. The mixtures never collapsed. The uniform mixture paid its log-grid price where effects were weak: it missed the power bar in two IRIS games and one TD-MPC2 task in which validation tuning reached it. In the IRIS and TD-MPC2 study the weighted mixture reached the bar in exactly the games and tasks in which validation tuning did, and it kept the uniform mixture’s protection on the ERK test fields, where validation tuning collapsed.

What to do in practice.

For anyone asking whether a world model trained on experimental data responds to actions, our results suggest five habits. First, do not read an action effect off replacement diagnostics; they answer a different question and are fooled by stand-in effects. Second, if actions were randomized, reconstruct the design law and resample from it conditionally on everything the design conditioned on; a resampler that is simpler than the design reintroduces the trap. Third, compute the design-only bound before opening any outcome; a deterministic protocol can never yield evidence, whatever the model. Fourth, when many sites share an action sequence, do not pool their log scores at face value, even when the score is the model’s own likelihood; temper them, and prefer a mixture over a fixed grid of factors to any single factor, estimated or tuned, since every single factor we tried failed somewhere. Weighting the mixture toward the factor chosen on validation data recovers most of that factor’s power at little risk. Fifth, give every negative control a statistic that has power, or an invalid resampler can go unnoticed.

The confirmatory evidence is narrow.

On biological data, our confirmatory test of the repaired statistic is one field of one dataset at one horizon. It detects an effect that biology already establishes, so it shows that the repaired test has power on real data, not that it discovers new effects; it says nothing about the size of the effect or about power in other systems. The thirty-minute horizon and the CcaS data were not part of that test. The registered tests on published world models (§9, §10) cover three model families, 26 Atari games and six control tasks, with random actions in simulators and a horizon of one step. They show that pooling amplification and its repair by mixtures carry over to models we did not build; they do not validate those models’ counterfactual predictions, they do not test the stand-in trap, and they reach weak effects only through partial execution.

The analysis was not blind, and part of it is post hoc.

The datasets had been analyzed before in our own earlier study, so M4 is a registered re-analysis rather than a blind test. The pooled statistic registered for M4 failed its positive controls; the diagnosis, the repair and the exploratory check X all followed that failure, and only M5 is confirmatory for the repair. The repair was selected on synthetic data under a pre-committed rule whose tie-resolution detail was implemented only after the evaluation; on this evidence the Kish-tempered and field-mean statistics are interchangeable. The sealed challenge’s designer had seen the source of the reference models. Every such departure is listed, with dates and hashes, in Appendix D.

Validity rests on assumptions about the design and the measurement.

Every guarantee is conditional on the working design law; for ERK it is a reconstruction whose exact acquisition rule is not verified for the confirmatory field, and every CcaS rejection is conditional on a one-step delay, consistent with a shift at data export, that was found after the first design checks failed. We calibrated the working laws on the released command records, but no theorem licenses them (Proposition 5). We also assume that the observation mask and segmentation do not respond to future actions. Designs whose logging policy reads past outcomes need the conditional product law of Assumption 2; reading another unit’s actions inside the block can violate that law, so a policy outside the sufficient construction of Proposition 12(b) needs a separate argument for its conditional law. The own-channel analyses carry a vacuous eligibility bound and are descriptive only.

The repairs have limits of their own.

The tests are conservative and have little power for effects that are masked at the level of each unit or that are weak relative to the design’s entropy. Contrast tempering restored power in the pixel world at the larger effect size, but even there without extracting the additional evidence that more pixels carry, so its e-values stayed far below the oracle’s; on published world models it repaired neither DIAMOND nor IRIS’s decoded pixels and failed on two of the six TD-MPC2 tasks, and we do not recommend it. The mixture can lose up to the logarithm of its grid size in log e-value relative to the best grid member, which can matter near the rejection threshold; it was weaker than contrast tempering and validation tuning at the smaller pixel effect, and it missed the power bar in two IRIS games and one TD-MPC2 task in which validation tuning reached it. The weighted mixture closes most of that gap, but trails validation tuning by up to log(4/3) when validation tuning is right. Its growth guarantee across precision scales also requires grid coverage and the moment-domain conditions of Proposition 8. Propositions 8–12 were written after the registrations and checked in several sessions of independent AI review (Appendix E), not by a human statistician. The pixel demonstration itself uses one simulator family, two model classes and one training run per cell, at reduced episode counts. Finally, a sharp-null rejection says that some site responds to some future action within the horizon; it does not say which, by how much, or through what mechanism. The authors used Claude (Claude Code and claude.ai) and Codex for code, drafting and review, and they verified all analyses and claims.

Outlook.

Three extensions would most strengthen the method: a registered test of the mixture on biological data with weak effects, which the ERK dataset analyzed here cannot provide (§8.6); statistics that recover the evidence pooling discards rather than merely discounting it—a joint Gaussian with a low-rank model of the residual covariance did not (§9.4); and designs that are randomized with these tests in mind, since the design-only bound shows that an experiment’s evidential capacity is fixed before any model is trained. More broadly, wherever world models are evaluated on data that cannot be replayed, the experiment’s own randomization is the only source of counterfactual truth, and it is worth using.

Appendix A BioWM-Eval

Both datasets of §8 were analyzed earlier in our BioWM-Eval study. This appendix states what that study measured, how its results relate to the tests of this paper, and what its records do and do not establish about its own analysis history. The quotations and figures below are taken from the committed revision package of that study (Appendix E lists the files and hashes).

What it measured.

BioWM-Eval defined the utility of future actions as the relative reduction in the best achievable squared prediction error when the future actions are added to the state and the clock, U∗​(h)=[R0∗​(h)−R1∗​(h)]/R0∗​(h)U^{*}(h)=[R_{0}^{*}(h)-R_{1}^{*}(h)]/R_{0}^{*}(h), and estimated it by comparing held-out risks of matched fitted models with and without the future actions. In its own words, this quantity depends on the information set and does not estimate a causal effect. For ERK it compared matched one-step ridge models with and without the next programmed light pulse, both using the same past values and clock terms, and forecast thirty minutes ahead; for CcaS/CcaR it used seven leave-one-date-out comparisons at the same horizon. The ERK gain on the original minimum-gap fields was 49.6%; the CcaS gain was 0.91%, below the study’s 2% practical cutoff, which was an internal decision rule fixed before the biological analyses and not a public preregistration.

How it relates to this paper.

A with-versus-without-actions forecast comparison is the kind of diagnostic whose apparent action effects §7 shows can arise from stand-in effects. Our rejections therefore neither validate the size of the ERK gain nor say anything about whether the CcaS gain is practically meaningful: the sharp-null tests ask whether any site responds to the future actions, not how much prediction improves. Where the two studies are mentioned together, the juxtaposition is descriptive. The original ERK and CcaS/CcaR studies had already demonstrated that these systems can be predicted or controlled; BioWM-Eval did not claim those biological findings as its own, and neither do we.

What its records establish.

BioWM-Eval’s biological analyses were sequential and exploratory; unlike its synthetic challenges, none had sealed inputs or a sealed evaluator. Before the clock-controlled ERK comparison, an earlier comparison without the matched state-and-clock baseline had already been run on the same two held-out experiments, with gains of 56.2% and 57.6%. A rule-freeze record precedes the first clock-controlled result by less than an hour, but it does not name that comparison as primary, and the original project kept no version history; whether the ERK comparison was designated primary before or after its first result therefore cannot be established. The study’s synthetic challenges were sealed and revealed in a recorded order, but the challenge author and the evaluator were operated by the same agent, so its “blind” evaluations reflect an internal sealed-input order, not independent human blinding or public preregistration. These facts are why we treat M4 as a re-analysis (§8.1) and why no BioWM-Eval figure is used as evidence in this paper.

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 Sources and changes relative to the frozen documents

The obligations P1–P4 of the registered specification are proved in two theory documents that are part of the registered code archive and were therefore fixed before the registration: a core document (P1(a)–(d), P1b, P2(a)–(e), P3, P4) and a calibration supplement (P1(e) and the template-avoidance recursion). A third note in the archive covers averaging across models. Table 8 lists them with their hashes; the files used here are byte-identical to the archived ones.

The proofs below follow these documents. Writing them for the paper, we made the following changes, none of which affects the registered method: [Added] the selection, training-independence and Monte Carlo hypotheses (i)–(iii) of Proposition 1, which the frozen proofs use implicitly, together with the frozen training and design information in the conditioning fields and the grid filtration; [Tightened] the conditioning field under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}} is written out explicitly, with the targets of units outside the independent set excluded; [Added] the hypotheses of Proposition 2(b) on the template list and on positive conditioning probability, and the derivation of the product path law from the per-origin design assumption; [Tightened] the approximate-law bound (Proposition 5), replacing a coupling argument by a direct total-variation bound conditional on the frozen baseline and defining Δ\Delta on the whole command path; [Tightened] the range of density ratios in Proposition 3 (r≥1r\geq 1, with the reversed case noted) and the conditioning on frozen training information in Proposition 4(c); [Added] for Proposition 6, the reading as independent and identically distributed copies at a fixed clock, the restriction of the frozen construction that the predictor’s window contains recent commands and constant outcomes but not the stratum, now stated in the proposition, and a written argument for its probability-one step for ideal predictors. Proposition 7 is new and is proved in §4.5.

Propositions 8–12 have no frozen counterpart: they were written after the registrations and checked by Codex, a model family different from the drafting model, in an independent review, a delta review of the revision, a check of the trap experiment’s logging policy, and a final check of the integrated text with a delta check of its revisions; the counterexamples are archived with the reviews (Table 16). Their proofs are in §B.8–§B.12.

Fix a residue rr and its grid t0<t1<…t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots, tk+1=tk+ht_{k+1}=t_{k}+h. Let 𝒢k=σ⁡(ℱtk,𝒯,𝒮,J,Ut0,…,Utk−1)\mathcal{G}_{k}=\sigma(\mathcal{F}_{t_{k}},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{S},J,U_{t_{0}},\dots,U_{t_{k-1}}), where UtjU_{t_{j}} are the independent auxiliary seeds that generate the Monte Carlo draws at tjt_{j}. Ville’s inequality gives Pr⁡(supk∏j<kXj≥1/α)≤α\Pr(\sup_{k}\prod_{j<k}X_{j}\geq 1/\alpha)\leq\alpha, and 𝔼⁡[∏j<τXj]≤1\mathbb{E}[\prod_{j<\tau}X_{j}]\leq 1 for every (𝒢k)(\mathcal{G}_{k})-stopping time τ\tau, by localization and Fatou’s lemma, with the product on {τ=∞}\{\tau=\infty\} read as the almost-sure limit of the non-negative martingale.

Averages and the batch test (part (c)).

A prechosen arithmetic average of non-negative random variables with expectation at most one has expectation at most one, without any assumption on their dependence; Markov’s inequality then gives Pr⁡(E≥1/α)≤α\Pr(E\geq 1/\alpha)\leq\alpha. Averages over independent sets or models of processes adapted to the same filtration are again martingales; processes of different residue classes are adapted to different grids, and on a common clock a class factor is not conditionally mean one once part of its block is revealed, so the class average is a fixed-time e-value only. For the batch test at one common origin, the observed joint block and the joint draws are exchangeable given 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} (all units under H0GH_{0}^{G}, one independent set under H0ownH_{0}^{\mathrm{own}}), and the observed-inclusive rank p-value that counts ties as exceedances is super-uniform.

B.3 Eligibility (Proposition 2)

Part (a).

Let Π∗\Pi^{*} be the pipeline that uses the structural eligibility events and Π^\hat{\Pi} the pipeline that uses command-based classifiers, run with the same statistics and Monte Carlo draws. Let DD be the event that any classifier decision differs from its structural event. On the complement of DD the two pipelines are identical. Hence, unconditionally,

Pr⁡(Π^​ rejects)≤Pr⁡(Π∗​ rejects)+Pr⁡(D)≤α+δ,\Pr(\hat{\Pi}\text{ rejects})\leq\Pr(\Pi^{*}\text{ rejects})+\Pr(D)\leq\alpha+\delta,

capped at one; distinct classifier errors may be combined by a union bound. No independence between classifier errors and assignments is needed. The bound does not hold conditionally on an observed selected set.

Part (b): from the per-origin law to the path law.

[Added] Let Ki,s(⋅∣Ai,≤s)K_{i,s}(\cdot\mid A_{i,\leq s}) be the one-step kernel of the design, with the fixed stratum suppressed.
